3 US Presidential Election Polling via Frequentist Methods

  1. 7.

    The UK General election was held on July 4th 2024. One day before, an opinion poll was published which was based on a sample of 1200 voters, of whom 294 indicated that they would vote Conservative. (We will assume that the sample was random; in fact it wasn’t.) Imagine that it is still July 3rd 2024, and suppose that p is the proportion of voters who will vote Conservative on July 4th 2024.

    1. (a)

      Based on the results from this particular opinion poll, what would be your estimate for p?

    2. (b)

      Let X be the random variable representing the total number of Conservative voters in a sample of size n drawn from the UK voting population. Write down the distribution of X, an approximate distribution for X, and an approximate distribution for the estimated proportion, p^=Xn.

    3. (c)

      If we require a margin of error of ±0.02 (i.e. 2%) in our opinion poll, how large should we choose n (assuming the worst case for the value of p)?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      We use the estimator p^ to estimate p, where p^=X/n, with n being the size of the sample. So once we have seen this polling data we have p^=294/1200=0.245=24.5%. Note that we also sometimes use the notation Y instead of p^.

    2. (b)

      X has a binomial distribution with parameters n=1200 and p unknown, so we write X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p). This assumes that the UK population is sufficiently large to make successive responses independent. The inferences that we intend to make depend on the sample being a simple random sample of UK voters. In fact, many opinion polls are not simple random samples but quota or other kinds of sample, which suffer from various disadvantages.

      Approximately, X∼N⁢(1200⁢p,1200⁢p⁢(1−p)) as n is very large, and we expect p to be not too far from 50%, ensuring both n⁢p and n⁢(1−p) should also be large. The sample proportion p^ also approximately has a Normal distribution: p^∼N⁢(p,p⁢(1−p)/1200).

    3. (c)

      Typically we think of the margin of error as about two standard deviations. For unknown n and p, two standard deviations here is 2⁢p⁢(1−p)/n. The worst case is when p=0.5, as the standard deviation is largest for p=0.5. In this worst case, the margin of error is thus 1/n. We thus require 1/n≤0.02, or n≥2500.

  2. 8.
    1. (a)

      We saw that if X is the sum of the successes in n Bernoulli trials with parameter p, then it has Binomial distribution X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p), with p.m.f. given by

      f⁢(x|n,p)={(nx)⁢px⁢qn−xfor⁢x=0,1,2,…,n,0otherwise.

      with q=1−p. Assuming that x and n are fixed and can hence be treated as constants (which incidentally would be the case if we had actually performed the trials and hence know n and x), find the value of p that maximises f⁢(x|n,p). Hint: you may want to examine log⁡f⁢(x|n,p) as it is easier to differentiate.

    2. (b)

      The value you found in part (a) can be considered an estimate for p and is usually denoted p^. Why do we use this notation: why not just call this value p?

    3. (c)

      The value of p^ you found in part (a) should agree with the expression for p^ we found in lectures, when we examined the p.m.f. of n Bernoulli trials f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) directly. Why must these results be the same? Hint: as part of your answer, you may wish to discuss the similarities and differences in the form of f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) compared to f⁢(x|n,p).

    Solution

    1. (a)

      We use the suggested trick of maximising the log of f⁢(x|n,p) as this is a little easier to differentiate:

      f⁢(x|n,p) = (nx)⁢px⁢qn−x (2)
      ⇒log⁡f⁢(x|n,p) = log⁡(nx)+x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (3)
      ⇒∂∂p⁢log⁡f⁢(x|n,p) = 0+xp−n−x1−p (4)

      therefore an estimate for p, which we denote p^, which maximises f⁢(x|n,p) is given by

      xp^−n−x1−p^ = 0 (5)
      ⇒x⁢(1−p^) = (n−x)⁢p^ (6)
      ⇒x−x⁢p^ = n⁢p^−x⁢p^ (7)
      ⇒x = n⁢p^ (8)
      ⇒p^ = xn (9)

      the sample proportion (as expected).

    2. (b)

      The answer is pretty much in the question (but it highlights a fundamental point): the notation p is reserved for the ‘true’ probability (or proportion if applicable). Our derived p^ is just an estimate for p: the fact that p^ maximises f⁢(x|n,p) is good, but does not make it perfect, so by definition it is not the same as p, hence the notation.

    3. (c)

      The p.m.f. of n Bernoulli trials is given by

      f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p)=px⁢qn−x (10)

      with xi=0 or 1 and x=∑i=1nxi (and 0 otherwise). Comparing to the Binomial p.m.f. f⁢(x|n,p), we see that if n and x are fixed, they both have exactly the same dependence on p. The only difference is the multiplicative factor of (nx) in the Binomial p.m.f.. This factor is irrelevant when maximising as it goes to zero as soon as we differentiate with respect to p, as can be seen in Equation (4), after which the two calculations for p^ perfectly agree. A more conceptual explanation can be seen by examining the form of f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) and seeing that it depends upon the results of the trials xi only via the total number of successes x. It hence does not change the probability for different orderings of the same number of successes x: the ordering brings no extra information besides what is contained in x (a result of the independence of the trials). Similarly, the Binomial p.m.f. is derived from the Bernoulli p.m.f., but is deliberately set up to ‘forget’ this ordering and hence also only depends on x. Therefore we would anticipate that the two calculations must give the same answer as they are essentially using the same information.

      This question is a teaser for the concept of sufficiency (here x is sufficient for all the xi) and of maximising the likelihood (here f⁢(x|n,p)), which we will return to later in the course.

  3. 9.

    [Exam standard] A US study in 1974-75 surveyed the attitudes of people to the role of women in society, stratified according to race and gender. In particular, individuals were asked whether or not they agreed with the statement

    Women should take care of running their homes and leave running the country up to the men.

    In all, 1566 women were surveyed. The number, X, of women in agreement with the proposition were counted.

    1. (a)

      Under what conditions is this a ‘binomial scenario’ (i.e. can it be thought of as the counts from a series of Bernoulli trials)?

    2. (b)

      Suppose that the proportion of US women in agreement with this proposition is 0.33. Find the probability that we see between 500 and 560 (inclusive) women in favour of this proposition.

    3. (c)

      Do you believe that a correction for continuity is useful for this example? If not, when might a continuity correction be more useful?

    4. (d)

      The actual number of women in agreement for this sample was 555. What is the probability of seeing a result as extreme (i.e. as far from the expected value in either direction, assuming p=0.33) as this?

    Solution

    1. (a)

      Binomial scenario: each woman’s view is considered an independent (Bernoulli) trial. We will consider agreement with the statement as “success”, and suppose that there is the same probability p that each woman will express agreement. Finally, we count X, the total number of women in agreement.

    2. (b)

      X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p)=B⁢i⁢n⁢(1566,0.33) so that E⁢(X)=n⁢p=516.78 and V⁢a⁢r⁢(X)=n⁢p⁢(1−p)=346.2426=18.612.

      Use a Normal approximation: approximately, X∼N⁢(n⁢p,n⁢p⁢(1−p))=N⁢(516.78,18.612). We require

      P⁢(500≤X≤560)=P⁢(500−516.7818.61≤X−516.7818.61≤560−516.7818.61)=P⁢(−0.90≤Z≤2.32),

      where Z is standard Normal. We have P⁢(−0.90≤Z≤2.32)=P⁢(Z≤2.32)−P⁢(Z≤−0.90)=P⁢(Z≤2.32)−P⁢(Z≥0.90)=P⁢(Z≤2.32)−(1−P⁢(Z≤0.90)). From tables, this evaluates to 0.9898−(1−0.8159)=0.9898−0.1841=0.8057.

    3. (c)

      Continuity correction would make little difference. Would be more worthwhile for a smaller value of n.

    4. (d)

      The observed count is 555, which is a distance of (555-516.78)=38.22 from the expected value. An observed count of (516.78-38.22)=478.46 or less would be just as far from the expected value. Thus, we require

      1−P⁢(478.46≤X≤555)=1−P⁢(−38.2218.61≤X−516.7818.61≤38.2218.61)=1−P⁢(−2.05≤Z≤2.05),

      which equals P⁢(Z≤−2.05)+P⁢(Z≥2.05)=2⁢P⁢(Z≥2.05)=2⁢(1−P⁢(Z≤2.05)) we find from tables is 2⁢(1−0.9798)=0.0404.

  4. 10.

    Suppose that a random variable X has a binomial distribution with parameters n and p, and consider the proportion p^=Xn. Prove that Var⁢[p^] is maximum at p=0.5.

    Solution   Let p^ be the random variable representing the sample proportion (note we sometimes use Y instead of p^). Consider the function g⁢(p)=Var⁢[p^]=p⁢(1−p)n; 0<p<1. To find turning points, differentiate with respect to p and equate to zero:

    g′⁢(p)=1−2⁢pn=0⇒p=0.5.

    To find out whether this is a minimum or a maximum, find the second derivative:

    g′′⁢(p)=−2n.

    As this is negative, the turning point is a maximum.

  5. 11.

    When p is small, the Normal approximation to the binomial distribution is not so useful. Instead, the Poisson distribution can be used. A random variable X has a Poisson distribution with parameter λ when its probability distribution is

    f⁢(x|λ)=P⁢(X=x)=λx⁢e−λx!,λ>0,x=0,1,2,…

    Here, X is a discrete random variable which can take the non-negative integers for its values. The Poisson distribution is typically used to model the number of times a particular event occurs over a specified period of time. The Poisson distribution is unusual in that it has the same mean and variance, namely λ. The link between the Poisson distribution and the binomial distribution is that, for large n and small p, X is approximately distributed Poisson with parameter λ=n⁢p. A guide as to when the approximation is useful is that we approximately need n>20 and n⁢p=λ<7.

    People with certain kinds of stomach illness may be referred to a specialist who will carry out a gastroscopy to identify whether or not the cause of the illness is gastric cancer. Amongst individuals referred to the specialist, the diagnosis of cancer is made in 0.7% of cases. The specialist sees about 150 patients per month. Find the probability that, in a given month, the specialist will diagnose more than two cases of cancer.

    Solution

    Approximate using Poisson with λ=n⁢p=(150)⁢(0.007)=1.05. Then,

    P⁢(X>2) =1−P⁢(X=0)−P⁢(X=1)−P⁢(X=2)
    =1−e−1.05⁢[1+(1.05)+(1.05)22]
    =0.0897.
